Variables & Types.exp: Variables and data types in Kotlin.

Input/Output.exp: Input and output operations in Kotlin.

What is Kotlin: Kotlin is a modern, statically-typed language that runs on the JVM, JS, and Native targets. It's concise, safe, and fully interoperable with Java.
Kotlin Syntax: Kotlin omits semicolons and uses `fun` for functions, `val` for read-only references, and `var` for mutable ones. Types come after colons.

val name: String = "Doge"
var age = 5
fun greet() = "Hello"
println("$name is $age")
Variables & Types: Kotlin infers types. `val` (immutable like final) and `var` (mutable). Basic types: String, Int, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Char, Byte, Short.

val pi = 3.14159
var counter = 0
val visible: Boolean = true
val items = listOf(1, 2, 3)
println(pi::class.simpleName)
Null Safety: Kotlin eliminates null pointer exceptions with nullable types (`?`), safe calls (`?.`), Elvis operator (`?:`), and the not-null assertion (`!!`).

var name: String? = null
println(name?.length)
println(name ?: "Default")
name = "Doge"
println(name!!.length)
Kotlin Playground: The Kotlin Playground is an online IDE to experiment with Kotlin code. It supports multiplatform targets, embedded snippets, and sharing via URLs.
Multiplatform Overview: Kotlin Multiplatform shares business logic across JVM, JS, iOS, Android, and Native. Write once in shared modules; platform code in target modules.
Project Structure: Standard Kotlin projects use Gradle with `src/main/kotlin` and `src/test/kotlin`. Multiplatform adds `commonMain`, `jvmMain`, `iosMain` source sets.

Project/
 ├── build.gradle.kts
 ├── settings.gradle.kts
 └── src/
    ├── main/kotlin/
    │   └── Main.kt
    └── test/kotlin/
        └── MainTest.kt
Kotlin/Native & WASM: Kotlin/Native compiles to native binaries (no JVM required) via LLVM. Targets: Windows (Mingw), Linux, macOS, iOS, Android NDK, WebAssembly. Use `konanTargets` in Gradle. Kotlin/Wasm targets WebAssembly with Kotlin/Wasm compiler. Native supports Kotlin's standard library subset, including coroutines and serialization.

If & When expressions: `if` and `when` are expressions that return values. `when` replaces Java's switch and supports smart casts, ranges, and arbitrary conditions.

val score = 85
val grade = when {
    score >= 90 -> 'A'
    score >= 80 -> 'B'
    else -> 'F'
}
val max = if (a > b) a else b
println(grade)
for & while Loops: `for` iterates over ranges, collections, or anything with an iterator. `while` and `do..while` work as expected. Ranges use `..`, `until`, `downTo`, `step`.
Range & Progression: Ranges (`1..10`) define intervals. Progressions control step direction. Use `in` to check membership, `until` for exclusive end.

val closed = 1..5
val half = 1 until 5
val descending = 5 downTo 1
val step = 0..10 step 2
println(3 in closed)
println(3 in half)
Equality Checks: `==` calls `equals()` (structural equality). `===` checks referential identity. `!=` and `!==` are the negated forms.

val a = listOf(1, 2)
val b = listOf(1, 2)
val c = a
println(a == b)   // true — structural
println(a === b)  // false — different references
println(a === c)  // true — same reference
Exception Handling: Use `try-catch-finally`. Kotlin has no checked exceptions. `catch` blocks can filter by exception type, and `finally` always executes.
try as Expression: `try` is an expression in Kotlin. It returns the last expression in the `try` block or the matching `catch` block. Use `finally` for side effects.
Ranges & Progressions: Ranges: `a..b` (inclusive), `a..<b` (exclusive, Kotlin 1.9+), `a downTo b`, `a..b step c`. Check containment with `in` operator. Progressions: IntProgression, LongProgression, CharProgression. Empty ranges: `10..1` (empty). `until` extension: `0 until 10` = `0..9`. Indices of collections. Iterate over ranges with for loops.

Function Declaration: Functions use `fun` with explicit return types. Expression bodies omit braces. Single-expression functions infer the return type automatically.
Default & Named Args: Parameters can have default values. Named arguments allow skipping or reordering parameters, improving readability for functions with many parameters.

fun createUser(name: String, age: Int = 18, active: Boolean = true) {}
createUser("Alice")
createUser("Bob", active = false)
createUser(age = 25, name = "Charlie")
Lambda & Higher-Order: Lambdas are function literals. Higher-order functions take or return functions. Trailing lambda syntax removes parentheses for clean DSL-like code.
Extension Functions: Add new functions to existing classes without inheritance. Extensions are resolved statically — they don't actually modify the class.

fun String.isEmail() = this.contains('@') && this.contains('.')
fun List<Int>.product() = fold(1) { acc, i -> acc * i }

println("test@example.com".isEmail())
println(listOf(2, 3, 4).product())
Infix Functions: Infix functions are called without dot or parens. Single-parameter member or extension functions marked with `infix`. Common in DSLs.

infix fun Int.times(str: String) = str.repeat(this)
println(3 times "Ha ")  // Ha Ha Ha

// Built-in: to
val map = mapOf(1 to "one", 2 to "two")
Operator Overloading: Kotlin allows overloading operators like `+`, `-`, `*`, `[]`, `()` via functions named `plus`, `minus`, `times`, `get`, `invoke`.

data class Vector(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    operator fun plus(other: Vector) = Vector(x + other.x, y + other.y)
    operator fun get(index: Int) = if (index == 0) x else y
}
val v1 = Vector(1, 2)
val v2 = Vector(3, 4)
println(v1 + v2)  // Vector(x=4, y=6)
tailrec: `tailrec` optimises recursive functions into iterative loops when the recursive call is in tail position. No stack overflow risk.
Inline Functions: `inline` inlines the function body at call sites, avoiding lambda object allocation. Use for higher-order functions with lambda parameters.
Destructuring Declarations: Destructuring decomposes an object into variables: val (name, age) = person. Works for data classes, Pair, Triple, Map.Entry, and classes with componentN() operators. Use _ for unused components. In lambdas: map.forEach { (key, value) -> }. Destructuring in for loops: for ((k, v) in map). ComponentN is an operator function: operator fun component1(): Type.

data class Person(val name: String, val age: Int)

fun main() {
    val person = Person("John", 30)
    val (name, age) = person
    println("$name, $age")

    val pair = "key" to "value"
    val (k, v) = pair

    val map = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2)
    for ((key, value) in map) {
        println("$key = $value")
    }

    val list = listOf(1 to "one", 2 to "two")
    list.forEach { (num, word) ->
        println("$num = $word")
    }

    val arr = intArrayOf(1, 2, 3)
    val (x, y, z) = arr
    println("$x, $y, $z")

    println(person.component1())
    println(person.component2())
}

Lists & Arrays: `listOf` creates read-only lists, `mutableListOf` for mutable. `arrayOf` for arrays. Lists are covariant; arrays are invariant.

val readOnly = listOf("a", "b", "c")
val mutable = mutableListOf("a", "b")
mutable.add("d")
val arr = arrayOf(1, 2, 3)
println(readOnly[1])
println(mutable)
Maps & Sets: `mapOf`/`mutableMapOf` for key-value pairs. `setOf`/`mutableSetOf` for unique elements. Immutable by default.

val map = mapOf("key1" to 1, "key2" to 2)
val set = setOf(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
val mutableMap = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
mutableMap["Doge"] = 5
println(map["key1"])
println(set)
Sequences: Sequences provide lazy evaluation for collection chains. Use `asSequence()` for large datasets to avoid intermediate list allocations.
Functional Operations: Kotlin provides rich functional APIs: map, filter, reduce, fold, flatMap, sortedBy, distinct, zip, unzip, associate, and more.

val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
println(nums.map { it * 2 })
println(nums.filter { it % 2 == 0 })
println(nums.fold(0) { acc, i -> acc + i })
println(nums.flatMap { listOf(it, -it) })
println(nums.associateWith { it * it })
Grouping & Partitioning: `groupBy` groups elements by a key selector. `partition` splits into two lists based on a predicate. `groupingBy` for eager grouping.
Windowed & Chunked: `chunked(size)` splits collection into fixed-size lists. `windowed(size)` creates sliding windows. Both support partial windows and steps.
Element Operations:
val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
println(nums.first { it > 1 })    // 2
println(nums.singleOrNull { it > 5 }) // null
println(nums.take(2))             // [1, 2]
println(nums.drop(2))             // [3, 2, 1]
println(nums.distinct())          // [1, 2, 3]
Sequences vs Iterables: Sequences (Sequence<T>) provide lazy evaluation: intermediate operations don't execute until terminal operation. Collections are eager. Use `.asSequence()` for chains of `map/filter/take` to avoid intermediate collections. Sequences are ideal for large datasets, infinite series, and chaining many operations. Generate with `sequence { yield() }`, `generateSequence`, `asSequence`.

Class Basics: Classes use `class` with a primary constructor in the header. Properties declared in the constructor are automatically generated with getters/setters.

class Person(val name: String, var age: Int)
val p = Person("Alice", 30)
println(p.name)
p.age = 31
Inheritance & Interfaces: Classes are final by default — use `open` to allow inheritance. Override methods with `override`. Interfaces can have abstract and default implementations.
Data Classes: `data class` automatically generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions. Perfect for DTOs and value objects.

data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)
val u1 = User(1, "Alice")
val u2 = u1.copy(name = "Bob")
println(u1)
println(u1 == User(1, "Alice"))
val (id, name) = u1  // destructuring
Sealed Classes & Interfaces: Sealed types restrict hierarchies to a fixed set of subclasses defined in the same file. Perfect for representing states or algebraic data types.
Object & Companion: `object` declares a singleton. `companion object` defines static-like members inside a class. Objects can also implement interfaces as anonymous instances.
Value & Inline Classes: `value class` wraps a single value without heap allocation overhead. Use `@JvmInline` for JVM interop. Prevents primitive boxing in many cases.
Type Aliases: Type aliases provide alternative names for existing types, improving readability without introducing new types. Useful for function types and complex generics.

typealias UserMap = Map<Int, User>
typealias Predicate<T> = (T) -> Boolean
typealias Callback = (Result) -> Unit

val users: UserMap = mapOf(1 to User(1, "Alice"))
val isAdult: Predicate<Int> = { it >= 18 }
Delegation: `by` delegates interface implementation to another object. `by lazy` for lazy initialization. Delegated properties via `observable`, `vetoable`, or custom delegates.
Abstract Classes & Nested: Abstract classes can have constructors, state, and both abstract and concrete methods. Nested/inner classes differ by whether they hold an outer reference.
Value Classes (Inline): Value classes wrap a single value with minimal overhead (no heap allocation in most cases). Declare with `@JvmInline value class`. Can have methods and computed properties but no backing fields, no `init` blocks, no class delegation. Inline classes replace primitive wrapper types with type safety. Also useful for type-safe IDs, units, domain primitives.

Generic Functions & Classes: Generics enable type-safe code with type parameters. Functions and classes can be parameterised with one or more type parameters.

class Box<T>(val value: T)
fun <T> List<T>.secondOrNull(): T? = if (size >= 2) this[1] else null

val intBox = Box(42)
val strBox = Box("Hello")
println(listOf(1, 2, 3).secondOrNull())
Variance — out & in: `out T` makes a type covariant (producer). `in T` makes it contravariant (consumer). Declaration-site variance avoids wildcards.
Reified Type Parameters: Reified type parameters (inline fun <reified T>) preserve generic type information at runtime. Works only with inline functions. Enables `T::class`, `is T`, `as T`. Bypasses JVM type erasure of generics. Common use: type-safe Gson/Jackson deserialization, type checks, `instanceof`-style pattern matching.
Star Projections: `*` for unknown type arguments. `MutableList<*>` is a mutable list of unknown type — safe to read as `Any?`, but not to write.
Type Bounds & Where: `T : UpperBound` constrains type parameters. Multiple bounds use `where` clause. Use `Nothing` for impossible values.

fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf(a: T, b: T) = if (a > b) a else b

interface Serializable
fun <T> copy(value: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Serializable
    = value

println(maxOf(3, 7))

Launch & Async: `launch` fires a fire-and-forget coroutine. `async` starts a coroutine that returns a `Deferred` result via `await()`. Both are non-blocking.
Dispatchers: Dispatchers determine thread pools: Default for CPU, IO for I/O, Main for UI, Unconfined for testing. `withContext` switches dispatchers.
Structured Concurrency: Coroutines lifetime ties to parent scope. Cancellation propagates downward; errors bubble up. `coroutineScope` waits for all children to complete.
supervisorScope: supervisorScope isolates child failures: one child's exception doesn't cancel siblings or parent. Use for parallel independent work.
Coroutine Context & Scope: CoroutineContext combines Dispatcher, Job, and elements. `CoroutineScope` manages lifecycle. `Job` tracks lifecycle of a coroutine.
Cancellation & Timeouts: Cancellation is cooperative — check `isActive` or use `yield()`. `withTimeout` throws TimeoutCancellationException. `withTimeoutOrNull` returns null.
Exception Handling: Uncaught exceptions cancel parent. Use `try-catch` inside coroutine, or `CoroutineExceptionHandler` for top-level exceptions.
coroutineScope vs runBlocking: `coroutineScope` suspends without blocking a thread. `runBlocking` blocks the current thread for bridge mode. Use coroutineScope in suspend functions.
Dispatchers & Threading: Dispatchers determine coroutine execution threads. Dispatchers.Default: CPU-bound work (thread pool = #cores). Dispatchers.IO: I/O-bound work (expandable pool). Dispatchers.Main: UI thread (Android, JavaFX). Dispatchers.Unconfined: runs in current thread until first suspension. `newSingleThreadContext`/`newFixedThreadPoolContext` for custom pools. `withContext` changes dispatcher within a coroutine.

Flow Basics: Flow is a cold async stream. Use `flow { }` builder with `emit()`, collect with `collect()`. Cold means nothing happens until collected.
Flow Builders: Additional builders: `flowOf` for fixed values, `asFlow` on collections/ranges, `channelFlow` for concurrent emission, `callbackFlow` for callback APIs.
Flow Operators: Intermediate operators: map, filter, transform, take, drop, debounce, sample, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest.
StateFlow: StateFlow holds observable state. Hot flow — always has a value. Emits only distinct values. Ideal for ViewModels and UI state.
SharedFlow: SharedFlow emits events to multiple collectors. Hot flow with replay cache. Use `MutableSharedFlow` for one-shot events like toasts.
CallbackFlow: callbackFlow bridges callback-based APIs into Flows. Use `send()` inside, `awaitClose()` to clean up. Context preserving.
Combining Flows: `zip` pairs elements one-to-one. `combine` merges latest values. `merge` interleaves multiple flows into one.
Flow Operators Deep: Flow operators: map, filter, transform, take, drop, distinctUntilChanged, debounce, sample, flatMapConcat/Merge/Latest, buffer, conflate, catch, retry, retryWhen, onCompletion, combine, zip. Terminal operators: collect, toList, toSet, first, single, count, reduce, fold. Operators are cold (start on collect). Use flowOn to change context. Buffer for concurrent processing. catch recovers from upstream errors.

Context Receivers: Context receivers declare dependency on context types without inheritance. Functions can receive multiple contexts for modular APIs.
Contracts: Contracts tell the compiler about function behavior. Use `callsInPlace`, `returnsNotNull`, `implies` for smarter analysis and fewer warnings.
@JvmInline & JvmAnnotations: `@JvmInline` marks inline classes on JVM. `@JvmStatic`, `@JvmOverloads`, `@JvmField`, `@Throws` control Kotlin-to-Java interop.
Type Erasure & Reified: JVM erases generic types at runtime. `inline` + `reified` preserves them. `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")` for manual casts.
Reflection: Kotlin reflection (`::class`, `::memberProperty`) inspects types at runtime. Use `memberProperties`, `functions`, `annotations` for meta-programming.

data class Person(val name: String, val age: Int)

val kClass = Person::class
println(kClass.simpleName)  // Person
println(kClass.memberProperties)

val prop = Person::name
val person = Person("Alice", 30)
println(prop.get(person))  // Alice
Annotations: Kotlin annotations: `@Target`, `@Retention`, custom annotation classes. Apply to classes, functions, properties, or expressions with `@file:`, `@get:` etc.
Destructuring Declarations: Destructuring decomposes objects into variables with `componentN()` functions. Data classes auto-generate them; custom classes can implement operator fun componentN().
Inline Functions & Performance: Inline functions copy their body to call sites, avoiding function call overhead. Use for lambdas (reduces object creation). `crossinline` prevents non-local returns, `noinline` prevents inlining specific parameters. `value class` + inline functions = zero-overhead abstractions. Over-inlining increases code size; use judiciously for small, frequently-called functions.

KMP Overview: Kotlin Multiplatform shares logic across platforms. Business logic, data models, and networking in commonMain; platform UIs in platform-specific source sets.
expect/actual: `expect` declares platform-agnostic API in common code. `actual` provides platform-specific implementations. Compiler ensures all expects have actuals.
Common Code: CommonMain uses Kotlin stdlib-common, kotlinx.coroutines, kotlinx.serialization. Shared data models, repository logic, and ViewModels live here.
Platform-Specific Code: Platform source sets (jvmMain, iosMain, jsMain) provide actual implementations. Access platform APIs and libraries from each target.
KMP Libraries & Frameworks: KMP has a growing ecosystem: Ktor for networking, SQLDelight for databases, Koin for DI, kotlinx.serialization, and Compose Multiplatform for UI.
expect/actual Mechanism: expect/actual declares platform-specific APIs. `expect` in common code defines the interface, `actual` in platform modules provides the implementation. Works for functions, properties, classes, objects, type aliases. Platform source sets: `commonMain`, `jvmMain`, `jsMain`, `nativeMain`, `iosMain`, etc. Use `@OptionalExpectation` for annotations.

kotlin.test Basics: `kotlin.test` provides `@Test`, `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertNull`, `assertThrows`. Annotations work with JUnit 4/5, and multiplatform testing.
Kotest: Kotest is a multiplatform test framework with behavior specs, property-based testing, matchers, and data-driven tests.
MockK: MockK is a Kotlin-first mocking library. Supports coroutines, spies, relaxed mocks, capturing, and verification with expressive DSL.
Property-Based Testing: Property testing verifies invariants across many random inputs. Kotest and kotlin-check use generators (`Arb`) and properties (`forAll`).
Coroutine Testing: `kotlinx-coroutines-test` provides `runTest`, `TestScope`, and virtual time. `advanceTimeBy`, `advanceUntilIdle` skip delays instantly.
JUnit 5 Integration: Kotlin works seamlessly with JUnit 5. Use `@ParameterizedTest`, `@MethodSource`, `@ValueSource` with Kotlin collections and lambdas.
Property Testing (Kotest): Kotest property testing generates random inputs to verify invariants. `forAll`, `forNone`, `forAtLeast`. Generators: `Arb.int()`, `Arb.string()`, `Arb.list(Arb.int())`. Custom generators with `arbitrary { }`. Shrinking finds minimal failing case. Combine with table testing for specific cases. IntSeededRandom for reproducibility.
Mocking with MockK: MockK is Kotlin's mocking library designed for Kotlin features: coroutines, extension functions, object mocks, private functions. Key features: `mockk<T>()`, `every { } returns`, `coEvery { } coReturns`, `verify { }`, `slot`, `capture`, `relaxed mock`. Use `mockkStatic` for companion/static, `spyk` for partial mocks. `confirmVerified` ensures all calls were verified.

Gradle Kotlin DSL: Gradle Kotlin DSL is the idiomatic build configuration for Kotlin projects. Uses `.gradle.kts` files. Type-safe accessors for configurations, tasks, extensions. Key plugins: kotlin("jvm"), kotlin("multiplatform"), kotlin("plugin.serialization"), application. Version catalogs (libs.versions.toml) for dependency management. Convention plugins for shared build logic.
Version Catalogs: Version catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` centralise dependency versions. Access via `libs.some.dependency` in build scripts.
buildSrc & Convention Plugins: buildSrc stores shared build logic as Kotlin sources. Convention plugins apply common configurations across modules — DRY for multi-module projects.
KSP & K2 Compiler: KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) is a compiler plugin for annotation processing. K2 compiler (1.9+) offers faster compilation and improved type inference.
Dokka & Tooling: Dokka generates Kotlin documentation (KDoc). Supports multiplatform projects, HTML/MD/JavaDoc outputs. Often used with Gradle's `dokka` plugin.

Scope Functions Deep: Scope functions: `let`, `run`, `with`, `apply`, `also`. Key differences: context object (it vs this), return value (context vs lambda result). `let`: `it` + result for transformations/chaining. `apply`: `this` + context for configuration. `run`: `this` + result for computing with context. `also`: `it` + context for side effects. `with`: `this` + result (extension function, non-null). Combine thoughtfully for readable code.
Lambda with Receiver: Lambda with receiver allows calling methods on an implicit `this` inside the lambda. The `receiver` type is the context. Used by `apply`, `run`, `with`, `buildString`, and custom DSLs. From Kotlin in Action.
Type-Safe Builders & @DslMarker: Type-safe builders use lambdas with receivers for declarative construction. @DslMarker restricts implicit receiver access to prevent ambiguity with nested builder contexts. Common: HTML builders, Gradle DSL, Compose UI. Builder pattern with apply/also. Context receivers (Kotlin 1.6+) for multiple receivers in scope.
SAM Conversion: Single Abstract Method (SAM) conversion lets you pass a lambda where a Java functional interface is expected. Kotlin has built-in function types, so SAM conversion mainly applies to Java interop. From Head First Kotlin.
Java Interop: Kotlin is 100% interoperable with Java. Key annotations: `@JvmStatic` for static methods, `@JvmOverloads` for overloaded methods, `@JvmField` for fields, `@Throws` for checked exceptions, `@JvmName` to resolve signature clashes.
Kotlin Idioms: Common Kotlin idioms from Head First Kotlin and Kotlin in Action: default arguments for builders, `require`/`check` for preconditions, `use` for Closeable, `takeIf`/`takeUnless` for conditional returns, `TODO()` for stubs, `runCatching` for try-catch expressions.

Jetpack Compose Basics: Jetpack Compose is Kotlin's declarative UI framework for Android. `@Composable` functions describe UI. State: `mutableStateOf`, `remember`, `derivedStateOf`, `collectAsState`. Layout: Column, Row, Box, LazyColumn, LazyRow. Modifier chain for styling. Side effects: LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect. Compose uses Kotlin coroutines for animations and async operations.
ViewModel & State: ViewModel survives configuration changes. Use `viewModel()` in Compose, expose `StateFlow`, and collect as Compose state with `collectAsState()`.
LiveData & StateFlow: LiveData is lifecycle-aware. StateFlow is the coroutines-native alternative. Use `asLiveData()` to bridge StateFlow to LiveData for legacy code.
Room Database: Room is a SQLite ORM. Use `@Entity`, `@Dao`, `@Database`. Coroutines support via suspend functions and Flow return types in DAOs.
Retrofit & Networking: Retrofit type-safe HTTP client used with Kotlin coroutines. Define `suspend` functions in API interfaces. Use kotlinx.serialization or Moshi for JSON.
Navigation Compose: Navigation Compose provides type-safe navigation in Compose. Define routes with `NavHost`, navigate with `navController.navigate()`, pass safe args.
Ktor Client & Networking: Ktor Client is Kotlin multiplatform HTTP client. Features: coroutine-based, pluggable engines (OkHttp JVM, Darwin iOS, JS), content negotiation, kotlinx.serialization, auth, cookies, WebSockets. Build with HttpClient { install(ContentNegotiation) { json() } }. Requests: get, post, put, delete. Streaming with HttpStatement.
